The System Protection Unit (SPU) protects peripheral configuration registers from
unintended writes. In systems with multiple processors and DMA controllers, the SPU
acts like a security guard, controlling who can modify critical peripheral settings.

> **Note**
>
> This guide applies to all ADSP-SC

Think of the SPU as a gatekeeper for peripheral registers. It sits between the
system bus and peripheral configuration registers, checking every write request.
If a write comes from an unauthorized source, the SPU blocks it.

Each peripheral has a dedicated protection register `SPU_WP[n]` that controls
which bus requesters can write to its registers. We can:

- Allow or block specific processor cores
- Allow or block DMA controllers
- Configure different permissions for each peripheral

The SPU can issue a system-wide lock signal that all peripherals recognize. When
enabled, any peripheral with its lock bit set will reject all write attempts to
its control register.

The SPU integrates with ARM TrustZone to enforce security boundaries:

- Secure peripherals only accept secure transactions
- Non-secure masters cannot access secure peripherals
- Each peripheral’s security level is configurable

The SPU can protect its own configuration registers, preventing unauthorized changes
to the protection settings. Once locked, only a system reset can restore access.

The SPU examines every write transaction in this order:

1. Destination Check - Which peripheral is being accessed?
2. Source Check - Which bus requester is requesting the write?
3. Permission Check - Is this master allowed to write to this peripheral?
4. Decide - Pass the write through, or return a

To protect a peripheral from writes by specific bus requesters, we need to configure several registers.

First, we should find the peripheral’s write-protect register number in the Hardware Reference Manual.

Second, we can set the corresponding bits in `SPU_WP[n]` for bus requesters we want to bloc

Global lock provides a quick way to simultaneously protect control registers
across multiple peripherals. This mechanism is controlled by registers both in SPU and others.
For example CDU_CTL register has LOCK bit to enable it. When we activate the global lock over
SPU_CTL by setting GLCK bit, the r

TrustZone security features apply to all SC5xx processors with ARM Cortex cores.
The SPU security register numbers match the WP numbers. This is controlled over
SSEC and MSEC bits under `SPU_SECUREP[n]` registers for peripherals. For cores, there is
`SPU_SECUREC[n]` register with `CSEC[n]` bits. For

Software can check if it’s running in secure or non-secure mode by examining the value of
`SPU_SECURECHK` register. The `SPU_SECURECHK` register reads by secure requesters return
`0xFFFFFFFF`. Reads by non-secure requesters return `0x00000000`.

To prevent any changes to SPU configuration until the next reset, we can even lock the SPU itself.
For this, we can set WPLCK and GLCK and also block all masters to SPUs own write-protect registers.
We need to be careful since this lock can only be unlocked with a reset.

The SPU can generate interrupts when a write is blocked.

We can configure the SPU to generate interrupts. This is controlled by the `PINTEN`
bit in the `SPU_CTL` register. After setting this bit, we can examine the `SPU_STAT`
register to see the details of the violation. Detailed instructions on ho

When a transaction is blocked, the SPU returns a bus error to the requesting master.
The master’s bus fault handler will be called. We can examine the `SPU_STAT` register to see the
details of the violation. Specifically, the LWERR, ADDRERR or VIRQ bits can be used to see
the details of the error. D

Key SPU registers:
|Register|Purpose|
|`SPU_CTL`|Control: Global lock, write-protect lock, interrupt enable|
|`SPU_STAT`|Status: Lock write errors, interrupts|
|`SPU_WP[n]`|Write-protect register for each peripheral (n = 0-202)|
|`SPU_SECURECTL`|Security control: Lock secure config, interrupt enable

- If you lock the SPU’s control register but forget to protect the SPU’s own
  WP register (WP121), someone can still modify the protection settings.

The ADSP-SC5xx processors include two important hardware protection
units that help secure and protect system resources from unintended access or modification.

The system protection features consist of:

- **System Protection Unit (SPU)** - Protects peripheral registers from
  unauthorized writes
- **System Memory Protection Unit (SMPU)** - Protects memory regions from
  unauthorized read/write access

  destabilize the system.

The ADSP clock architecture is made up of a few core hardware blocks that are
responsible for generating and routing core system clocks throughout the SoC.
The exact clock trees between SoCs can vary however they share a common
structure between them, allowing customers to configure system clocks to

The CGU is responsible for generating all core system clocks used throughout
the ADSP SoCs, it is made up of various core parts such as the PLL
(phased-locked loops), divider clocks and clock gating control. The ADSP SoCs
have two CGU blocks, CGU0 and CGU1. By default core system peripherals are
clo

The Clock Distribution Unit (CDU) selects and routes clocks generated by the
CGUs to core SoC peripherals. Each CDU output (`CLKO[n]`) contains a
multiplexer that selects one of up to four possible input clocks, along with
clock gating functionality used to enable or disable the output. Each
`CLKO[n

The initial ADSP clock configuration is programmed by U-Boot during early
system initialisation before Linux has started. U-Boot configures the CDU
followed by the CGU during this phase. The CDU initialisation selects the
reference clock used by CGU1 and programs the initial input clock
selection an

Linux provides several `debugfs` interfaces that can be used to inspect the
ADSP clock configuration. The Linux common clock framework provides a summary of the Linux
clock topology, while the ADSP CDU driver provides access to the current CDU
hardware register state.

The Linux common clock framework exposes `clk_summary` through `debugfs`.
This provides an overview of the clocks registered with Linux, including their
parent relationships, enable states, and current clock rates.

To view the clock summary:

```console
$ cat /sys/kernel/debug/clk/clk_summary
```

The ADSP CDU driver exposes a register dump through `debugfs` for CDU
specific clock debugging. The dump provides the live CDU register state,
including input clock selection, output enable state, and CDU status
information.

To view the CDU register dump:

```console
$ cat /sys/kernel/debug/clk/cdu

The System Memory Protection Unit (SMPU) provides flexible protection of memory
regions against unauthorized read or write access. Think of it as a security
checkpoint for memory. This peripheral examines every memory transaction and
decides whether to allow or block it.

> **Note**
>
> This guide a

The SMPU protects specific memory regions from unauthorized read or write
transactions by specific cores and DMA requesters. We can configure:

- Which memory regions to protect
- Whether to protect reads, writes, or both
- Which bus requesters are allowed to access each region
- Whether secure or n

- **Multiple SMPU Instances** - Each processor family has multiple SMPU
  instances protecting different memory paths; the number and configuration
  varies by family.
- **Multiple Protection Regions** - Each SMPU instance can monitor up to 8
  memory regions simultaneously, each with its own size a

Make sure you’re configuring the right SMPU instance for the memory path you want
to protect; L2 memory has multiple SMPU instances. An example from SC59x is given below.

|Instance|Location|What It Protects|
|SMPU-CL2_0|L2 Core Port 0|L2 SRAM Banks 0-3, Boot ROM0|
|SMPU-DL2_0|L2 DMA Port 0|L2 SRAM Banks 0-7, Boot ROM0-2|
|SMPU-CL2_1|L2 Core Port 1|L2 SRAM Banks 4-7, Boot ROM1-2|
|SMPU-DL2_1|L2 DMA Port 1|L2 SRAM Banks 0-7, Boot ROM0-2|
|SMPU-CL2_2|L2 Core Port 2|L2 S

The SMPU examines every memory transaction in this order:

1. Address Check - Does it fall within a protected region?
2. Operation Check - Is it a read or write?
3. Bus Requester ID check - Which bus requester is making the request?
4. Security Level Check - Is it a secure or non-secure transaction?

To protect a memory region, we need to configure several registers.

First, we should define the region to protect. This can be done by setting the
base address and size in `SMPU_RADDR[n]` and `SMPU_RCTL[n]`.

Second, we need to configure the protection itself. After deciding whether we allow
read/w

As described above, each bus requester has a unique ID that the SMPU uses to control access.

(for example, the ARM cores are omitted). See the applicable

SMPU allows us to set region size between 4KB and 4GB. Each size has an address alignment requirement.
If the address is not properly aligned, the SMPU will mask the lower bits. It may end up with
potentially protecting a different region than intended. Some of the valid region sizes and their
align

Here, secure and non-secure refer to the corresponding ARM TrustZone transaction
states. We can control whether these transactions are allowed by writing to the
`SMPU_SECURECTL` register. As default, only secure transactions are allowed. To
also support non-secure transactions, we can set `WNSEN` an

We can also configure the security for individual regions by writing to
`SMPU_SECURERCTL[n]`. Each register covers one region (selected by `n`) and
consists of 4 bits: read/write permission crossed with secure/non-secure access.

The SMPU can forward read requests to memory before checking permissions,
saving one clock cycle. However, this may cause side effects for memory-mapped
registers that change state when read (like FIFOs that auto-clear). This is controlled
by `RSDIS` bit in `SMPU_CTL` register. When protecting memor

We can configure the SMPU to generate interrupts. This is controlled by the `PINTEN`
bit in the `SMPU_CTL` register. After setting this bit, we can examine the `SMPU_IADDR`
and `SMPU_IDTLS` registers to see the details of the violation. Detailed instructions on
how we can handle interrupts can be ex

Bus errors are enabled as default. We can disable them by setting the `PBEDIS` bit in the
`SMPU_CTL` register. When a transaction is blocked and bus error generation is enabled, the
SMPU returns an error to the requesting master. The master’s bus fault handler will be called.
We can examine the `SMP

SMPU allows us to protect the configurations we created by providing a lock mechanism. This lock
is simply the `LOCK` and/or `RLOCK` bits under `SMPU_CTL` register. If we lock the configs,
they are protected until SPU releases global lock.

Key SMPU registers for each region n (0-7):
|Register|Purpose|
|`SMPU_CTL`|Control: Lock, interrupts, bus errors, read speculation|
|`SMPU_STAT`|Status: Interrupts, errors, overruns|
|`SMPU_RADDR[n]`|Region base address (bits 31:12)|
|`SMPU_RCTL[n]`|Region control: Size, enable, read/write protectio

  your mask matches only the intended IDs.
- After reset, only secure transactions are allowed. If you’re running non-secure
  code, you must enable non-secure transactions or you’ll be blocked.
